sections.section_title: Introduction to Mudrās in Bharata-nātyam and Āgama
sections.content: This introductory section discusses the ancient convention of representing gods and goddesses in Bharata-nātyam using mudrās. It establishes the origin of these mudrās in Tantra and Āgama iconographic texts. The text explains that Āgamic worship rests on four pillars (catuṣpāt): mūrti (visualization), mantra (sacred formula), maṇḍala (diagram), and mudrā (hand gesture). It highlights that Bharata-nātyam has drawn heavily from this tradition, stylizing mudrā-hastās to signify the presence of a deity. The section also describes the 'pūrva-raṅga', a preliminary sequence in Bharata's Natyā-śāstra, which involves propitiating gods for a successful performance. It names various deities and celestial beings and their roles in protecting the theatre, such as Viśva-karmā (architect), Mitra (presiding over the green-room), and Varuṇa (presiding over upper realms).
sections.summary: The section introduces deity-specific mudrās, tracing their origins from Tantra and Āgama traditions to their stylized use in the classical dance form of Bharata-nātyam. It explains the foundational role of mudrās in Āgamic worship and describes the 'pūrva-raṅga' ritual from the Natyā-śāstra, where deities are invoked to bless a performance.

sections.section_title: Catalogue of Mudrās from Nandikeśvara's Abhinaya-darpaṇa
sections.content: This section references Nandikeśvara's 'Abhinaya-darpaṇa' as a source for specific mudrās for stellar divinities (graha) and gods/goddesses (deva). It states that the mudrās adopted by Bharata-nātyam dancers follow the weapons (āyudha), functions, and characters described in Āgama texts and Purāṇas. The core of this section is a large table detailing the mudrās (hastas) for both the left and right hands for a variety of deities. [TABLE: Lists mudrās for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śiva-liṅga, Sarasvati, Lakṣmī, Pārvati, Gaṇeśa, and Ṣaṇmukha.] The table continues with specific sets of hastas: 'Dikpāla-hastas' for the ten guardians of the directions, 'Nava-graha-hastas' for the nine celestial bodies, and 'Daśāvatāra-hastas' for the ten primary incarnations of Viṣṇu, plus one for Manmatha.
sections.summary: This part of the chapter presents a systematic catalogue of deity-specific mudrās, primarily drawing from Nandikeśvara's 'Abhinaya-darpaṇa'. It features a comprehensive table that lists the specific left-hand and right-hand gestures for major Hindu deities, the guardians of the directions (Dikpālas), the nine celestial bodies (Nava-grahas), and the ten avatars of Viṣṇu (Daśāvatāras).

sections.content: This section explains the function of the two main groups of mudrās. The first group of 55 (deity-specific ones) are used to visualize (cintana), enter into communion with (yoga), contemplate (dhyāna), and facilitate the recitation of mantras (japa) for the deities. The remaining 53 are for ritual acts like fetching articles for worship. It describes two commonly employed mudrās for all deities: sampuṭa and añjali. The text provides Sanskrit verses (ślokas) and descriptions for their formation. It also defines 'vandani-mudrā' (when añjali or sampuṭa is on the head) and 'mahā-mudrā' (when it is near the ear). It then lists and defines, with ślokas, other general mudrās like sammohana-mudrā, dhenu-mudrā, kūrma-mudrā, and yoga-mudrā.
sections.summary: The text categorizes the 108 traditional mudrās into two groups: 55 for deity worship and 53 for other ritual acts. It elaborates on the spiritual purpose of the deity-specific mudrās, which aid in visualization, communion, and contemplation. It then provides detailed descriptions and Sanskrit definitions for common, all-purpose mudrās like sampuṭa, añjali, dhenu, and yoga-mudrā.

sections.section_title: Mudrās for Minor Divinities and Gurus from Tantra-sāra
sections.content: Drawing from the 'Tantra-sāra', this section describes mudrās for minor divinities and figures of reverence. Each mudrā is presented with a Sanskrit śloka, an English description, and sometimes an illustration. The mudrās covered are: Vighna-rāja mudrā (for eliminating obstacles), Guru-saptaka-mudrā (obeisance to seven masters), Guru-pāduka-mudrā (representing the master's feet), Loka-pāla-mudrā (for the guardians of directions), and Kṣetra-pāla-mudrā (for the protector of the sacred site).
sections.summary: This section details specific mudrās for minor divinities and gurus, sourced from the 'Tantra-sāra'. It provides descriptions, Sanskrit verses, and illustrations for gestures used to eliminate obstacles (Vighna-rāja), show reverence to the lineage of masters (Guru-saptaka), honor the immediate guru (Guru-pāduka), and invoke the guardians of directions (Loka-pāla) and the protector of a sacred site (Kṣetra-pāla).

sections.content: This extensive section details the nineteen mudrās used in the worship of Viṣṇu. These mudrās represent Viṣṇu's aspects: weapons (conch, discus, mace, lotus), decorations (śrī-vatsa, kaustubha), vehicle (Garuḍa), incarnatory forms (Narasiṁha, Varāha), and unique forms like Kṛṣṇa (flute) and Rāma (bow, arrow, axe). Each of the nineteen mudrās is presented with its name, a line-drawing illustration, a defining Sanskrit śloka, and a detailed English description of how to form the gesture. The mudrās described include Śaṁkha, Cakra, Gadā, Padma, Veṇu, Śrī-vatsa, Kaustubha, Vanamālā, Jñāna, Bilva, Gāruḍa, Narasiṁha, Vārāha, Hāyagrīva, Dhanur, Bāṇa, Paraśu, Trailokya-mohana, and Kāma.
sections.summary: A detailed exploration of nineteen distinct mudrās associated with the worship of Viṣṇu. Each mudrā, representing an attribute, weapon, or incarnation of the deity, is systematically presented with an illustration, a Sanskrit verse defining its form, and a clear English explanation of the hand gesture. This section serves as a practical guide to the iconography of Viṣṇu in mudrā form.

sections.content: This section focuses on the ten mudrās prescribed for the worship of Śiva. It states that most of these represent the weapons and attributes of Śiva, such as the trident (triśūla), rosary (akṣa-mālā), and skull-cup (kapāla). The two exceptions are 'liṅga' and 'yoni'. The section then describes each of the ten mudrās: Liṅga, Yoni, Triśūla, Akṣa-mālā, Vara (boon-bestowal), Abhaya (protection), Mṛga (deer), Khaṭvāṅga (magical weapon), Kapāla (skull-cup), and Ḍamaru (hand-drum). Each description is accompanied by an illustration, a Sanskrit śloka, and an English explanation.
sections.summary: This section covers the ten primary mudrās used in Śiva worship. It explains that these gestures primarily symbolize Śiva's iconic attributes and weapons, as well as fundamental concepts like the liṅga and yoni. Each mudrā is individually detailed with an illustration, a Sanskrit verse, and a description of its formation and meaning.

sections.content: This section details the seven mudrās used in the worship of Gaṇapati (Gaṇeśa). These mudrās resemble the articles typically found in Gaṇeśa's hands: tusk, noose, goad, battle-axe, pomegranate, and sweet ball (laddu). The mudrās described are: Danta (tusk), Pāśa (noose), Aṅkuśa (goad), Vighna (obstacle), Paraśu (battle-axe, noted as already described), Laḍḍu (sweet ball), and Bījapūra (pomegranate). Each has an illustration, a śloka (or reference), and a description.
sections.summary: This part describes the seven mudrās specific to the worship of Gaṇapati. The gestures are iconographic, representing the deity's characteristic attributes like his tusk, the noose and goad he carries, and the sweets he enjoys. The mudrās are explained with illustrations and Sanskrit verses.

sections.content: This section discusses mudrās current among Śākta groups, representing the weapons carried by the Goddess in her various forms (Durgā, Kālī, etc.). It lists several, noting that some (noose, goad, boon-bestowal, protection, bow, arrow) have already been described. It then focuses on explaining the mudrās for a sword (Khaḍga), shield (Carma), ploughshare/pestle (Musala), and a mudrā named after Durgā herself. The text also includes two full pages of illustrations showing additional Śakti mudrās without detailed descriptions in the main text, such as Ardha-yoni, Mahāyoni, Pāśa, Lelihā, Muṇḍa, Caturaśra, Mudgara, Kālakarnī, Cāpa, Nārācha, Bhaga, and Puṭaka.
sections.summary: The section on Śakti mudrās covers gestures used by worshippers of the Divine Mother. These mudrās represent the weapons and power of the Goddess in her manifold forms like Durgā and Kālī. It provides details for the sword, shield, and pestle mudrās, and includes numerous illustrations of other relevant gestures.

sections.content: A brief section dedicated to the mudrā for Lakṣmī, the goddess of wealth. It is described as being formed from the Cakra-mudrā, with the fore-fingers stretched out and little fingers joined with the thumbs. An illustration and a Sanskrit śloka are provided.
sections.summary: This short section details the specific mudrā for Lakṣmī, the goddess of wealth. The gesture, a modification of the Cakra-mudrā, is explained with an accompanying illustration and Sanskrit verse.

sections.content: This section covers the four mudrās used in the worship of Sarasvatī, the goddess of learning. They represent a rosary (akṣa-mālā, already explained), lute (vīņā), exposition (vyākhyā), and scripture (pustaka). The Vīṇā, Pustaka, and Vyākhyāna mudrās are then detailed with illustrations, ślokas, and descriptions.
sections.summary: This section outlines the four mudrās for Sarasvatī, the goddess of learning. It provides detailed explanations for the gestures representing the lute (vīņā), scripture (pustaka), and exposition (vyākhyāna), all central to her iconography.

sections.content: This section is dedicated to five mudrās especially dear to the tantrik goddess Tārā. The five are listed as yoni-mudrā, bhūtini-mudrā, bīja-mudrā, daitya-dhūmini-mudrā, and lelihāna-mudrā. Since the first three have been described elsewhere, it provides details for Daitya-dhūminī (also called Dānava-dhūmaketu-mudrā, for liberation from fetters) and Lelihāna (the 'licking' gesture).
sections.summary: Five mudrās specific to the tantrik goddess Tārā are presented. The text focuses on providing detailed descriptions for two unique mudrās: Daitya-dhūminī, for liberation, and Lelihāna, a 'licking' gesture, while referencing previously explained mudrās.

sections.content: This section details the mudrās employed in the worship of Tripurā, the mother-goddess of the Śrī-cakra. It enumerates ten mudrās from the 'Vāmakeśvara-tantra' that represent the divinities in the enclosures of the Śrī-cakra. Each of the ten mudrās is then presented with an illustration, a śloka, and a description. The mudrās are Saṁkṣobha, Vidrāviṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Vaśaṁkarī, Unmādinī, Aṅkuśa (Mahāṅkuśa), Khecarī, Bīja, Yoni, and Trikhaṇḍā.
sections.summary: Focused on the worship of the goddess Tripurā within the Śrī-cakra tradition, this section systematically describes the ten specific mudrās sourced from the Vāmakeśvara-tantra. Each mudrā, corresponding to a divinity within the Śrī-cakra, is explained and illustrated in detail.

sections.content: A brief section that introduces other mudrās suggested for the sequence of nyāsa (ritual placement of deities/mantras on the body). It illustrates and describes two such mudrās: Saubhāgya-daṇḍinī-mudrā and Ripu-jihvā-graha-mudrā.
sections.summary: This short section introduces two mudrās specifically used for 'nyāsa', the ritualistic placing of mantras on the body. It illustrates and explains the Saubhāgya-daṇḍinī and Ripu-jihvā-graha mudrās.

sections.content: This section provides a second, more detailed set of descriptions for the mudrās of the nine stellar bodies (Nava-grahas), which were previously listed in the table on page 3. It explains that propitiating these demi-gods is a custom of great antiquity. Each of the nine grahas is given a mudrā with a śloka and/or description: Sūrya (sun), Candra (moon - 'ardha-dhenu'), Aṅgāraka (Mars - 'samīlanī'), Budha (Mercury - 'kuṇḍa-mudrā'), Bṛhaspat (Jupiter - 'cakra-mudrā'), Śukra (Venus - 'śūla-mudrā'), Śanaiścara (Saturn - 'siṁha-mukhī-mudrā'), Rāhu ('go-mukha-mudrā'), and Ketu.
sections.summary: Revisiting the mudrās for the nine celestial bodies (Nava-grahas), this section provides more detailed descriptions and Sanskrit verses for each gesture than the initial table. It outlines the specific mudrās used in the ancient practice of propitiating these stellar divinities.

sections.content: This section addresses the mudrās for the guardians of directions (dik-pālas), who are frequently worshipped. It lists the ten regents: Indra (East), Agni (South-East), Yama (South), Nirṛti (South-West), Varuṇa (West), Vāyu (North-West), Kubera (North), Ananta (below), and Brahmā (above). It provides a Sanskrit śloka that names ten mudrās required for dikpālaka-pūjā: Proannāma, Unnamana, Bimba, Paśupata, Śuddha, Tyāga, Sādhanī, Prasādhanī, a mudrā made with bent fingers, and Ugramudrā.
sections.summary: This section deals with the worship of the Loka-pālas, the guardians of the ten directions. It names the regents and provides a Sanskrit verse listing ten specific mudrās that are required for their collective worship (dikpālaka-pūjā).

sections.content: The final section discusses the mudrā for the seven mother-goddesses (Sapta-mātṛkās): Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaishṇavī, Vārahī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā. It describes the recommended mudrā, known as 'tri-mukh', where the thumb, fore-finger, and middle-finger of the right hand are joined at the top, and the other two fingers are doubled up.
sections.summary: The concluding section describes the 'tri-mukh' mudrā, which is recommended for the worship of the Sapta-mātṛkās, the seven mother-goddesses who are propitiated in many religious rites. The formation of this single mudrā for the group is explained.

chapter_summary: Chapter Three, 'DEITY-SPECIFIC MUDRĀS', provides a comprehensive encyclopedic overview of the hand gestures (mudrās) used in Hindu worship and classical dance, specifically Bharata-nātyam. It traces their origins to Tantra and Āgama texts, explaining their function in visualizing and communing with deities. The chapter systematically catalogues a vast array of mudrās, beginning with a large table from Nandikeśvara's 'Abhinaya-darpaṇa' for major deities, the Daśāvatāras, the Nava-grahas, and the Dikpālas. It then delves into detailed descriptions, each accompanied by Sanskrit verses, English explanations, and line-drawing illustrations, for specific divine pantheons: Viṣṇu (19 mudrās), Śiva (10 mudrās), Gaṇapati (7 mudrās), Śakti, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Tārā, and Tripurā (10 mudrās). The chapter concludes by describing mudrās for collective worship of the Nava-grahas, Loka-pālas, and Sapta-mātṛkās, serving as both a theoretical and practical guide to this aspect of Hindu ritual and iconography.
key_arguments: The mudrās used in the classical dance form of Bharata-nātyam are not merely decorative but are drawn from a deep and ancient religious tradition rooted in Tantra and Āgama texts.

Mudrās are a fundamental component of Āgamic worship, forming one of the four 'props' (catuṣpāt) alongside mūrti, mantra, and maṇḍala, and are essential for visualizing, communing with, and contemplating deities.
The iconography of Hindu deities is systematically encoded in specific hand gestures, with mudrās representing their weapons, attributes, forms, and functions.

There is a highly structured and codified system of mudrās for nearly every major and minor deity or divine group within the Hindu pantheon, from Viṣṇu and Śiva to the guardians of directions and the seven mother-goddesses.
key_takeaways: Mudrās are a sophisticated symbolic language connecting ritual, worship, and performance art.
A vast and specific vocabulary of hand gestures exists for representing different deities and their aspects.
The practice of using mudrās is textually supported by authoritative works like the Natyā-śāstra, Abhinaya-darpaṇa, and various Tantras and Āgamas.
Understanding these mudrās provides insight into the iconography, mythology, and worship practices associated with each deity.

quotations.quote:
अष्टोत्तरशतं मुद्रा ब्रह्मणा याः प्रकीर्तिताः ।
तासां तु पञ्चपञ्चशदेताः ग्राह्यास्तु पूजने ॥
शेषास्तु या स्त्रिपञ्चाशन्मुद्रास्ताः समयेषु च।
quotations.context: Stated after the table of mudrās, explaining that out of 108 mudrās declared by Brahmā, 55 are for worship (pūjane) and the other 53 are for other occasions (samayeṣu).

quotations.quote:
द्रव्यानयन सङ्केत नटनादिषु ताः स्मृताः ॥
देवानां चिन्तनें योगे ध्याने जप्ये विसर्जने ।
आद्यास्तु पञ्चपञ्चाशन्मुद्रा भैरव कीर्तिताः ॥
quotations.context: Explaining the purpose of the two groups of mudrās. The latter group is for fetching items and for dance (naṭana), while the first 55 are for contemplation (cintana), yoga, meditation (dhyāna), and mantra recitation (japya).

quotations.quote:
एकोनविंशतिर्मुद्रा विष्णोरुक्तामनीषिभिः ।
शंखचक्रगदापद्मवेणुश्रीवत्सकौस्तुभाः ।।
वनमाला तथा ज्ञानमुद्रा बिल्वाह्वया तथा।
गरुडाख्या परा मुद्रा विष्णोः सन्तोषवर्धिनी ।।
नारसिंही च वाराही हायग्रीवी धनुस्तथा ।
बाणमुद्रा ततः परशुर्जगन्मोहनिका परा ।।
काममुद्रा परा ख्याता ........।
quotations.context: Introducing the 19 mudrās of Viṣṇu by listing them.

quotations.quote:
शिवस्य दशमुद्रिकाः ॥
लिङ्ङ्गयोनि त्रिशूलाख्या मालेष्टाभीमृगाह्वयाः ।
खट्वाङ्ङ्ग च कपालाख्या डमरुः शिवतोषदाः ।।
quotations.context: Introducing the 10 mudrās of Śiva by listing them.

quotations.quote:
दशका मुद्रिका ज्ञेयास्त्रिपुरायाः प्रपूजने ।
संक्षोभद्रावणाकर्षवश्योन्मादमहाङ्कुशाः ।
खेचरी बीजयोन्याख्या त्रिखण्डा परिकीर्तिताः ॥
श्रुणु देवि प्रवक्ष्यामि मुद्राः सर्वार्थसिद्धिदाः।
याभिर्विरचिताभिस्तु सान्निध्यं त्रैपुरं भवेत्।।
quotations.context: Introducing the 10 mudrās of the goddess Tripurā, enumerating them and stating their power to bring about her presence.

tables_and_charts.description: A multi-part table listing deity-specific hand gestures (mudrās or hastas) for the left and right hands.
tables_and_charts.data_summary:
The table is organized into four sections: 
1. Major Deities: Lists mudrās for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śiva-liṅga, Sarasvati, Lakṣmī, Pārvati, Gaṇeśa, and Ṣaṇmukha.
2. Dikpāla-hastas: Lists mudrās for the eight guardians of the directions (Indra, Agni, Varuṇa, Yama, Vāyu, Kubera, Nṛṛti, Īśāna).
3. Nava-graha-hastas: Lists mudrās for the nine celestial bodies (Sūrya, Candra, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu, Ketu).
4. Daśāvatāra-hastas: Lists mudrās for the ten avatars of Viṣṇu (Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, etc.) and also for Manmatha.

images_and_diagrams.description: Line drawing of a hand gesture.
images_and_diagrams.significance: Illustrates the physical form of a specific mudrā discussed in the text. This is repeated for almost every mudrā described.

images_and_diagrams.description: A full-page compilation of line drawings for various Śakti mudrās: ARDHA-YONI-MUDRĀ, MAHĀYONI-MUDRĀ, PĀŚA-MUDRĀ, LELIHĀ-MUDRĀ, MUṆḌA-MUDRĀ, CATURAŚRA-MUDRĀ, MUDGARA-MUDRĀ.
images_and_diagrams.significance: Provides visual references for additional mudrās used in the worship of Śakti.

images_and_diagrams.description: A half-page compilation of line drawings for various Śakti mudrās: KĀLAKARṆĪ-MUDRĀ, CĀPA-MUDRĀ, NĀRĀCHA-MUDRĀ, BHAGA-MUDRĀ, PUṬAKA-MUDRĀ.
images_and_diagrams.significance: Provides further visual references for Śakti mudrās.

alternative_viewpoints.context: On page 19, after describing one Vārāha-mudrā, the text states, 'These are two alternative mudrās.' It then describes another and also mentions a third, 'nissanka-mudrā', which is suitable for both Narasiṁha and Varāha. This shows that there isn't always a single, universally accepted mudrā for a deity.

alternative_viewpoints.viewpoint: Varying Iconographic Conventions for Abhaya and Vara mudrās
alternative_viewpoints.context: On page 27, when describing the Abhaya-mudrā, the text notes, 'The left hand (palm showing) held with the fingers pointing upward and stretched out is the gesture of protection. In iconography, however, it is usual for the right hand to assume the gesture of protection and for the left the gesture of boon-bestowal.' This highlights a difference between textual prescription and common iconographic practice.
